tool.name: Thermal tester and electrical tester
tool.measures: the thermal conductivity (heat) and the electrical conductivity of the stone
tips: Press the tip flat on a clean facet
The thermal tester does not tell diamond from moissanite
Then move on to the electrical tester

steps.title: Diamond conducts heat
steps.text: Diamond is the best known conductor of heat: it carries heat away faster than copper. This is what makes it feel “cold” to the touch. The thermal tester (the Diamond Selector) slightly heats the tip of a probe, presses it on the stone and measures how fast the heat goes away. A diamond carries it away quickly; most imitations (cubic zirconia, glass, synthetic spinel) hold it back.

steps.title: Moissanite confuses the test
steps.text: Synthetic moissanite (silicon carbide) also conducts heat very well. A thermal tester therefore cannot tell it from diamond: it answers “diamond” in both cases. Synthetic diamonds (HPHT and CVD) are real diamonds too: they conduct heat like natural diamond.

steps.title: The electrical tester
steps.text: Diamond is an insulator: it does not conduct electricity. Synthetic moissanite, on the other hand, does conduct. The electrical tester (Moissanite/Diamond) passes a weak current through the tip: if current goes through, it is not a diamond. It is the test that tells these two stones apart.

steps.title: What to conclude?
steps.text: • Low heat: an imitation (glass, cubic zirconia, etc.). • High heat and current that goes through: a moissanite. • High heat and current blocked: a diamond, natural or synthetic. To know whether this diamond is natural or made, other instruments are needed (see the lesson on the diamond in the laboratory).

steps.title: To remember
steps.text:
• The thermal tester spots diamond, but confuses moissanite with it.
• The electrical tester separates moissanite from diamond.
• Neither says whether the diamond is natural or synthetic.
